glossary.html: Terminology and sources The map reuses vocabulary that Birgitta Böckeler set out in Harness engineering for coding agent users on martinfowler.com, adds a few working names of its own, and leans on ordinary engineering words for the rest. This page says which is which, so a reader moving between the two vocabularies can translate. All (35) Adopted from source (8) Adapted from source (4) Coined here (16) Common engineering usage (7) Translation table Böckeler's vocabulary on the left, the vocabulary used here on the right. "Adapted" means the idea is hers and the word or scope is different here. Böckeler / Thoughtworks Used here Relation Harness Harness (wide sense: the whole engineering environment) adopted Guides (feedforward controls) Skills, constitution, readiness questions adapted Sensors (feedback controls) Validators, tests, review skill adapted Computational controls Deterministic machinery; validators; gates adapted Inferential controls Probabilistic machinery; the review skill; harness evaluations adapted Regulation categories (maintainability, architecture, behaviour) Not used as categories; rules carry a route instead (gate / judgment / guidance) different Steering loop Feedback path, with its conversions named adapted Harnessability Give the agent a usable starting point; brownfield pre-flight analysis adapted Ambient affordances Not used; closest is the kit's technology profile different Harness templates Engineering Kit technology profiles adapted — Rule registry, evidence record, could_not_run, risk tier, workflow, software factory coined AI SDLC Common engineering usage The software development lifecycle (SDLC) with AI agents doing part of the work in every phase, from intent and specification through design, build, verification, release and operation, while deterministic checks and human decisions stay where they are needed. Not to be confused with two nearby uses. First, the lifecycle for building AI and machine-learning systems themselves: data preparation, model training and evaluation, deployment and monitoring for drift, which IBM calls the AI lifecycle. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. Source IBM — What Is the AI Lifecycle? IBM — AI-DLC: The AI-Driven Development Lifecycle AWS Builder Center Harness Adopted from source Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. Source Birgitta Böckeler — Harness engineering for coding agent users Birgitta Böckeler — Context Engineering for Coding Agents Harness engineering Adopted from source The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; OpenAI's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating model (software factory). Source Birgitta Böckeler Ryan Lopopolo Guides and sensors Adopted from source Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. In Böckeler's terms guides ↔ skills, constitution, readiness questions; sensors ↔ validators, tests, review skill Source Birgitta Böckeler Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Adapted from source Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. In Böckeler's terms computational ↔ deterministic; inferential ↔ probabilistic Source Birgitta Böckeler Steering loop Adopted from source Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. In Böckeler's terms steering loop ↔ feedback path Source Birgitta Böckeler Feedback path Adapted from source The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. Source Birgitta Böckeler Harnessability Adopted from source The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. Source Birgitta Böckeler Harness template Adopted from source Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. In Böckeler's terms harness template ↔ Engineering Kit technology profile Source Birgitta Böckeler Engineering Kit Coined here A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills, evaluation scenarios, evidence schema, commands and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration). Not an industry term. Rule registry Coined here One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) Coined here The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. Gate (deterministic gate) Common engineering usage A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the quality command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. Source Martin Fowler Paula Paul, Rosemary Wang Deterministic floor Coined here The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a quality command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a handful of validators for rules the team has already been hurt by, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. Validator Adapted from source A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency-cruiser, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. In Böckeler's terms validator ↔ computational sensor Source Birgitta Böckeler Skill Common engineering usage Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. In Böckeler's terms skill ↔ guide (feedforward control) Review skill Adapted from source An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. It proposes; it cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. In Böckeler's terms review skill ↔ inferential sensor Source Birgitta Böckeler Harness evaluation (eval) Common engineering usage A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? Distinct from application tests. Repeated when prompts, skills, tools or models change. This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. Evidence record Coined here What a run leaves behind without anyone writing it: change and configuration revisions, kit version, each check with its status and report link, agent findings, decisions pending, overall status. Its schema is fixed by the kit and is the one thing a project cannot customise. could_not_run Coined here A first-class result state, distinct from failed and skipped: the check was required but its prerequisite was missing (a tool absent from the runner image, an environment unavailable). Blocks on its own cause. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. Adapter Coined here The thin binding between the kit's core and one tool: an execution surface (where the agent runs), a change host (where the pull request lives) or a pipeline runner (where checks run unattended). The test of an adapter is how little is in it. Mechanism versus meaning Coined here The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. Workflow Coined here One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when it has run repeatedly, leaves evidence each time and has a metric. Three roles (agent, checks, people) Coined here The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. Workflows fail when these blur: an agent treated as verifier, or people treated as checks. Risk tier Common engineering usage Assigned at readiness or planning; selects which checks and which reviewers apply. The workflow definition stays the same, its cost scales with the change. A low tier never removes an applicable rule. Failure path Coined here A defined response to an interruption: a check detects a violation, a required check cannot run, a requirement is ambiguous, an agent finding is rejected, an exception is requested. A test failure and an unavailable environment need different responses; treating either as a pass misrepresents the evidence. Evidence hand-off Coined here Workflows are built one at a time but read each other's records: the readiness record configures verification, the verification record feeds release readiness, the release record is what an incident review reads. Evidence carries its scope with it and expires when the revision changes. Software factory Coined here Not a product or a platform: the operating model that appears when enough workflows share rules, evidence and feedback, so that what production teaches changes what specification asks. The industrial sense (identical outputs from a fixed process) is explicitly not what is meant. Review fatigue Common engineering usage More workflows, more evidence and more agent output landing on the same few approvers. Leading indicators: review latency, reviewer concentration, shortening comments. The answer is moving every mechanical check into a gate so reviewers see only decisions and exceptions. Skill erosion Common engineering usage What happens when agents do all the implementation and all the first drafts: the team stops getting the unaided repetitions that keep judgment sharp, and the factory depends on that judgment at every human decision point. Spec-driven development Adopted from source Making expected behaviour and constraints explicit before implementation, in a sequence from intent through specification, clarification, plan and tasks. This site treats it as the process spine the harness wraps around, and stays neutral on which tool supplies it. Source GitHub Specification readiness Coined here Enough clarity to proceed responsibly, with remaining uncertainty made visible. A workflow whose trigger is a spec marked ready for planning, whose checks are structural, whose decision is the product owner's, and whose output is a readiness record later workflows read. Independent basis for verification Coined here If an agent generates both the implementation and its tests from the same incomplete understanding, both may share the same mistaken assumption. Verification needs something defined apart from the implementation: acceptance criteria, access rules, interface contracts, representative data, failure scenarios. The export example Coined here The running hypothetical: a feature that lets users export customer records. Open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure, audit), an access rule (R-042 / SEC-004), a background worker with a broader query, a 50k-row load scenario, a volume-limit rule (R-017). It is the site's one worked example: a page that needs an example follows this change, so the abstractions can be checked against one story. Requisite variety Adopted from source Ashby's law: a regulator can only control a system if it has at least as much variety as the system it governs. Böckeler uses it to explain why committing to a narrow topology makes an agent easier to harness: restricting what the agent may produce shrinks the space the controls must cover. It is also the reason this site recommends starting with fewer controls than feel sufficient, on a few well-defined execution surfaces. Source W. Ross Ashby Birgitta Böckeler
index.html: Reference · edition 1.3.0 The AI SDLC Map The AI-assisted software lifecycle, from spec to software factory, on one page. A vendor-neutral reference for the AI SDLC: the software development lifecycle (SDLC) with AI agents doing part of the work in every phase. One map in five bands (context, lifecycle, core, enablement and assurance) and an adoption path, with every source named. See the map Browse the workflow catalog 5 bands 5 adoption stages 35 catalogued workflows 35 terms, each with its origin The map Context sets the risk tier; the lifecycle says where the work runs; the core does the work; enablement makes it possible; assurance proves it. Underlined labels open the page that covers them; or start by purpose below the map. ⤢ The AI SDLC Map A one-page map of the AI-assisted software lifecycle in five bands. 1 Context: project, product and flow type set the risk tier (HIL is hardware-in-the-loop testing, OTA over-the-air updates, CVE a published vulnerability). 2 Lifecycle: SAFe levels (portfolio, Agile Release Train, team; WSJF is weighted shortest job first, PI a planning interval), phases from idea to operate with the workflow in each, Definition of Ready (DoR) and Definition of Done (DoD), and a traceability spine from requirement to incident. Incident feedback loops back to change what Specification asks. 3 Core: harness engineering as the discipline, the Engineering Kit as the artefact, workflows as the unit of work, and the software factory as the operating state that emerges. 4 Enablement: agent runtime and tools (MCP is the Model Context Protocol), people and roles (PO / PM: product owner / product manager), and the operating model. 5 Assurance: evidence and traceability, standards and AI governance (templates include ADRs, architecture decision records), and measurement. A footer shows the adoption path: deterministic floor, one workflow, a second workflow with hand-off, feedback path proven, factory emerges. Credit lines in the footer name the sources of borrowed terms. The AI SDLC Map Five bands. Context sets the risk tier; the lifecycle says where; the core does the work; enablement makes it possible; assurance proves it. 1 · CONTEXT what kind of work Together these set the risk tier: which gates run, how deep, who approves. PROJECT TYPE Greenfield Brownfield Modernisation / migration brownfield starts with pre-flight analysis PRODUCT TYPE Web / cloud app Firmware / device Data & ML models Platform / shared lib changes which gates make sense (HIL, OTA, drift) FLOW Full feature Bug fix Hotfix * Trivial / config Spike / research Refactor / tech debt Dependency / CVE fix Migration · rollback * hotfix: expedited path, evidence completed afterwards, never skipped 2 · LIFECYCLE where it runs SAFe levels, phases, the workflow in each phase, Definition of Ready / Done, and the traceability spine underneath. Portfolio epics · WSJF · lean budgets Agile Release Train features · PI planning · system demo Team stories · iterations · DoR / DoD incident feedback changes what Specification asks Idea Specification Design Develop Build QA security · performance Deploy Release Operate DoR DoD intake & triage spec readiness design conformance pull-request verification · security & performance checks by tier deploy verification release readiness incident feedback requirement spec task test change release incident TRACEABILITY SPINE · linked by rule IDs Inspect & Adapt each PI: which workflow to add or tighten next 3 · CORE what does the work Built-in quality: gates enforce what a machine can check. DISCIPLINE Harness engineering what the agent may do, what a machine checks, what a person decides ARTEFACT Engineering Kit rule registry, validators, skills with evals, evidence schema, adapters UNIT OF WORK Workflows one decision end to end, with evidence; e.g. pull-request verification OPERATING STATE Software factory emerges when workflows share rules, evidence and feedback 4 · ENABLEMENT what makes it possible Tools, people and the operating model. The kit enforces policy; it never holds authority. AGENT RUNTIME & TOOLS Coding agents and agentic IDEs; model providers Tool access (MCP), sandboxes, permissions, secrets Spec-driven development (SDD) frameworks CI runner and change host, bound by thin adapters PEOPLE & ROLES PO / PM own intent and open decisions Architects own rules; QA owns scenarios and evals Engineers direct, verify, turn lessons into gates Platform team owns the kit Watch: review load, skill erosion, adoption OPERATING MODEL Scrum / Kanban teams on an Agile Release Train PI cadence, system demo, Inspect & Adapt Work tracking & knowledge base Decision rights and approvals; policy wins 5 · ASSURANCE what must be provable Every workflow run leaves an evidence record. Auditors, release and incident review all read the same one. EVIDENCE & TRACEABILITY Evidence record on every run, fixed schema Rule IDs link rule → check → decision passed · failed · skipped · could_not_run Valid for one revision; a new push expires it STANDARDS & AI GOVERNANCE Templates: spec, plan, ADR, release notes SOC 2 change controls; domain standards as they apply AI use policy: data sent to models, IP of generated code Agent permissions reviewed as privileged access MEASUREMENT Baseline before changing anything Flow metrics and DORA delivery metrics Escaped defects; reviewer load and concentration Cost per change, including tokens and evals ADOPTION PATH 0 Deterministic floor 1 One workflow 2 Second workflow + hand-off 3 Feedback path proven 4 Factory emerges Harness engineering, feedback path and validators: after Böckeler (martinfowler.com) Spec-driven development: after GitHub Spec Kit · Lifecycle terms: SAFe (Scaled Agile, Inc.) Each stage has something to build, something to measure, and a condition for moving on. ⤢ Adoption path: one step at a time, one workflow at a time Five adoption stages left to right: 0 Deterministic floor, 1 One workflow, 2 Second workflow and hand-off, 3 Feedback path proven, 4 Factory emerges. For each stage the diagram lists what to build, what to measure, a suggested condition for moving on, and a failure pattern to watch for. The order is the point: skills, agents and platforms added before the floor and the first workflow tend to become sprawl. A credit line in the footer names the sources of borrowed terms. Adoption path: one step at a time, one workflow at a time Companion to the one-page map. Each stage has something to build, something to measure, and a condition for moving on. STAGE 0 Deterministic floor BUILD A quality command that runs the same way locally and in CI Suggested: 3–5 validators for rules the team has already been hurt by Rule registry: every rule gets an ID, a route and an owner Evidence schema; branch protection actually enforced MEASURE Baseline: lead time, review time, escaped defects Share of rules still guidance-only MOVE ON WHEN Every merge passes the same checks, and enforcement is verified, not assumed. WATCH FOR Skipping straight to skills and agents on top of no gates. STAGE 1 One workflow BUILD Pull-request verification end to end Review skill with an evaluation set before it ships Risk tiers; failure paths including could_not_run Expected checks recorded before results MEASURE Reviewer minutes per PR Blocks by checks vs by people Agent finding acceptance rate MOVE ON WHEN Suggested: run on 20+ real changes, evidence every time, one measure better than baseline. WATCH FOR A demo-quality skill with no evals treated as a gate. STAGE 2 Second workflow + hand-off BUILD Specification readiness as the Definition of Ready Risk tier set at spec, read by verification Readiness record consumed automatically MEASURE Work returned for clarification Time waiting on decisions MOVE ON WHEN Verification reads readiness evidence without anyone copying it across. WATCH FOR Each workflow inventing its own evidence format. STAGE 3 Feedback path proven BUILD Incident review converts findings: criterion, test, validator or eval Inspect & Adapt reviews which conversions landed Kit versioned; changes go through the kit's own tests MEASURE Repeat defect categories Conversions closed vs opened MOVE ON WHEN Suggested: each of the last three incidents changed an upstream check. WATCH FOR Retro actions that are written down and never close. STAGE 4 Factory emerges BUILD Shared registry and evidence across workflows A second team installs the kit and passes its first feature Named owner for the connections between workflows MEASURE Requirement-to-release time Escaped defects vs throughput Cost per change incl. tokens and evals MOVE ON WHEN A second team adopts the kit without the original author in the room. WATCH FOR Building the platform before the workflows exist. Feedback path, validators and review skills: after Böckeler (martinfowler.com) · Inspect & Adapt: SAFe term (Scaled Agile, Inc.) The order is the point. Skills, agents and platforms added before the floor and the first workflow tend to become the sprawl they were meant to prevent. workflow-catalog.html: SDLC workflow catalog Every candidate workflow across the software development lifecycle (SDLC), using the definition in the terminology : it supports one delivery decision end to end, with a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. Each one is mapped one-to-one to the traditional activity it absorbs, so a reader can see that almost nothing here is new; the mechanical part moved to a check, the reading and drafting moved to an agent, and the decision stayed with a person but now carries evidence. 35 workflows 9 phases 3 floor 20 first 12 later 123 traditional activities mapped Map Table Traditional map Maturity All Floor First Later Change type All UI API Data Maturity Floor — Deterministic checks only, no agent needed, build first First — First workflows to run end to end Later — Needs evals, environments or organizational readiness that usually does not exist yet Sources for the traditional side: Process reference map (7 phases × 6 roles), Secure development lifecycle activities, Software testing life cycle, Agentic vs traditional SDLC loop, Six-phase SDLC model, Seven-phase process model, Gated feature release pipeline.
